subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is meant by an ecosystem?
options: The interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment
A single population of one species
Only the animals in an area
questions.explain: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living (biotic) organisms with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. Organisms depend on one another for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal (interdependence).

questions.q: A stable community is one in which:
options: The species and environmental factors are in balance so population sizes remain fairly constant
questions.explain: In a stable community all the species and environmental factors are in balance, so population sizes remain roughly constant over time.

questions.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor that can affect a community?
questions.explain: Abiotic (non-living) factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH, CO2 and wind. Biotic (living) factors include food availability, new predators, competition and pathogens.

questions.q: A cactus has a thick waxy layer, spines instead of leaves and stores water. These are examples of:
options: Structural adaptations to reduce water loss and survive in a dry habitat
questions.explain: These are structural adaptations helping the cactus survive in dry conditions: reduced surface area (spines) and a waxy layer reduce water loss, and stored water helps survival. Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional.

questions.q: Organisms that live in extreme environments such as hot springs or deep-sea vents are called:
questions.explain: Extremophiles are organisms (often bacteria) adapted to live in extreme conditions of temperature, pressure or salt concentration, such as deep-sea vents and hot springs.

questions.q: In a food chain, what do the arrows represent?
options: The transfer of energy/biomass from one organism to the next
The order in which organisms die
questions.explain: Arrows in a food chain show the transfer of energy and biomass from one organism to the next as it is eaten. Food chains begin with a producer (usually a plant or algae) that makes glucose by photosynthesis.

questions.q: In a predator-prey relationship, if the number of prey increases, what usually happens to the predator population?
options: It stays exactly the same forever
It increases because there is more food, then the two cycle
questions.explain: If prey increase, predators have more food, so the predator population rises. More predators then reduce the prey, which later reduces predators. This produces cyclical predator-prey population changes.

questions.q: A student uses a 0.25 m2 quadrat and finds an average of 4 daisies per quadrat in a field of 800 m2. What is the estimated total number of daisies?
questions.explain: Density = 4 / 0.25 = 16 daisies per m2. Total = 16 x 800 = 12800 daisies. Random quadrat sampling estimates population size, while transects show how distribution changes across a gradient.

questions.q: Why should quadrats be placed randomly when estimating a population?
options: To avoid bias so the sample fairly represents the whole area
To count only the largest plants
So all quadrats land on the same spot
questions.explain: Placing quadrats randomly (e.g. using random coordinates) avoids bias, so the sample is representative and the population estimate is more reliable. A transect is used to study how distribution changes across an environmental gradient.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere in the carbon cycle?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis by plants and algae removes CO2 from the atmosphere and locks carbon into glucose and other compounds. Respiration, combustion and decomposition return CO2 to the atmosphere.

questions.q: How is carbon in a dead animal returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide?
options: By decomposers (microorganisms) respiring as they break it down
questions.explain: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste. As they respire, carbon is released back to the atmosphere as CO2, recycling carbon for use in photosynthesis.

questions.q: The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining to the sea. Which process turns liquid water into water vapour?
questions.explain: Energy from the Sun evaporates water (and plants lose water vapour by transpiration). The vapour rises, condenses to form clouds, and returns as precipitation (rain/snow), providing fresh water on land.

questions.q: Which conditions increase the rate of decomposition by microorganisms?
questions.explain: Decomposers work fastest in warm, moist, well-oxygenated (aerobic) conditions. Gardeners use these conditions in compost bins. In airless (anaerobic) conditions, decay produces methane biogas.

questions.q: Biogas generators produce methane fuel. What conditions do they require? (Biology-only content)
options: Aerobic conditions with plenty of oxygen
Anaerobic (airless) conditions and a suitable temperature
questions.explain: Biogas (mainly methane) is produced by anaerobic decay of waste material by microorganisms. Generators need airless (anaerobic) conditions and a warm temperature to keep the microorganisms active.

questions.q: Which is a possible effect of environmental change on the distribution of species?
options: Species distribution is never affected by the environment
Changes in temperature, water availability or gases can cause species to migrate or decline
Distribution only depends on the time of day
questions.explain: Environmental changes such as temperature, availability of water, and the composition of atmospheric gases can affect where species can survive, causing their distribution to change (e.g. migration or local decline).

questions.q: What does biodiversity mean?
options: The variety of all the different species of organisms in an ecosystem or on Earth
The amount of carbon dioxide in the air
The total mass of one species
The number of humans in an area
questions.explain: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth or within an ecosystem. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and less dependent on any one species.

questions.q: Which human activity reduces biodiversity by destroying habitats?
questions.explain: Deforestation and destroying peat bogs (often for farmland or fuel) destroy habitats and release CO2, reducing biodiversity. A rising human population and higher standard of living increase resource use, waste and pollution.

questions.q: Which of these helps to maintain biodiversity?
options: Breeding programmes for endangered species and protecting habitats
questions.explain: Ways to maintain biodiversity include breeding programmes for endangered species, protecting and regenerating rare habitats, replanting hedgerows and forests, reducing deforestation, and recycling rather than landfill.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of biomass is transferred from one trophic level to the next? (Higher/biology content)
questions.explain: Only about 10% of the biomass from each trophic level is transferred to the level above. Biomass is lost through not all being eaten, egestion (faeces), and respiration/movement, which is why food chains are usually short.

questions.q: Which is a factor threatening global food security?
options: Rising human population, changing diets, new pests/pathogens and cost of farming
Reducing the human population to zero
questions.explain: Food security is threatened by the increasing human population, changing diets in wealthier countries, new pests and pathogens, environmental changes and the cost of farming inputs. Efficient food production and sustainable fishing help maintain supply.
